To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the crystalloid P-proteins of legume sieve tubes are reversibly regulated calcium-activated stopcocks.
P-protein crystalloid stopcocks in legumes are reversibly controlled by Ca2+ and that their dispersal is triggered when the plasma membrane is damaged.
crystalloids of leguminous sieve tubes can reversibly occlude the sieve tube lumen, and this occlusion is regulated by calcium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of P-proteins, the characteristic proteinaceous crystalline inclusions of sieve elements in higher plants.
the function of the P-protein crystalloid in the sieve elements of legumes.
the structure, function, and evolution of the sieve elements in higher plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the crystalloids are stopcocks that are regulated by Ca2+ and other cations.
P-protein crystalloid dispersal is induced by plasma membrane damage, osmotic stress, or Ca2+ influx and is reversed by chelation of divalent cations.
crystalloid dispersal is a reversible process, which can be induced by mechanical damage and by turgor fluctuations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
P-protein crystals in sieve tubes can reversibly occlude the phloem pathway.
the P-proteins of legumes represent a reversible stopcock in the sieve tube.
the sieve tubes of the leguminous plant Vicia faba L. contain reversible stopcocks, which can be activated by mechanical injury, osmotic stress or divalent cations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sieve tubes of Fabaceae are equipped with reversible calcium-regulated stopcocks.
P-proteins are not just static, they can move and they can be regulated.
sieve tubes of legumes are equipped with reversible stopcocks, which allow for the regulation of sieve tube conductivity.
